# The same servers on local Kubernetes

The lab's Postgres images also run unchanged as pods on a local Kubernetes cluster, so the
concurrency tests in the [pgvector notebook](../notebooks/pgvector_playground.ipynb) can run against
a pod as well as against compose. Every local cluster here is a container inside Docker Desktop's VM,
on the same cores as compose, which means a comparison between the two measures only what
Kubernetes networking and pods add.

## kind, k3d and k3s

kind runs stock Kubernetes in a container, k3d runs k3s
(a trimmed Kubernetes distribution) through its own command-line tool, and k3s can also run in a
single container started from Python. Each one exposes the two Postgres pods on its own pair of
ports:

```bash
just k8s-up kind     # stock Kubernetes, ports 5434 / 5435
just k8s-up k3d      # k3s through k3d, ports 5436 / 5437
just k8s-up k3s      # k3s in one container from Python, ports 5438 / 5439
just k8s-test kind   # the pgvector notebook against the cluster
```

| | kind | k3d |
|---|---|---|
| distribution | stock Kubernetes, built with kubeadm | k3s: one binary, SQLite datastore, trimmed components |
| node image | `kindest/node`, 1.3 GB | `rancher/k3s`, about 250 MB |
| cluster create | about 60 s with the image local | about 15 s after the first pull |
| host ports | mapped straight onto the node container | on a separate load-balancer container |
| loading a local image | `kind load docker-image` | `k3d image import` |
| extras by default | none | Traefik ingress and a local-path storage class |

The benchmark gives the same result on either cluster, so the choice comes down to whether stock
Kubernetes matters (kind) or a small cluster that starts quickly is enough (k3d).

## k3s from Python

Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes can only be switched on in its settings, and kind's node needs
kubeadm to run inside it, so neither can be started from the Docker SDK (docker-py). k3s can, because
it is a single binary that bootstraps the whole cluster by itself, which is also why k3d is only a
thin wrapper around the Docker client. `k8s/k3s.py` does the same job as k3d in about 150 lines of
docker-py:

1. It runs `rancher/k3s` as a privileged container and waits for the node.
2. It streams images in from the local Docker cache (`docker save` into `ctr images import`), so
   nothing is pulled twice.
3. It drops the manifests into k3s's auto-deploy directory, which k3s applies on its own, so no
   `kubectl` call is needed.
4. It waits for the pods, and for Postgres to answer on the host port.

A cold start takes about 40 seconds, and about 10 when the container already exists. When the
pgvector notebook is pointed at `k3s-pg16` it calls the script itself, so the Kubernetes run works on
a clean machine with only Docker installed.
